blocks.text: A Nigerian pays federal income tax, obeys state road traffic edicts and pays a local government market levy — three governments, one citizen. A Ghanaian answers to one national government and its appointed district assemblies. The difference has a name: federalism.

blocks.markdown: This classification asks a different question from the presidential-parliamentary one. Instead of asking how the executive relates to the legislature, it asks **how power is distributed between the centre and the geographical units**.

blocks.title: The three arrangements
blocks.text: A UNITARY system concentrates all constitutional power in one central government, which may delegate functions to local units but can withdraw them at will. A FEDERAL system divides powers between a central government and component units by a written constitution, so that each is supreme in its own sphere. A CONFEDERAL system is a loose union of sovereign states in which the centre exercises only the powers the units choose to give it and may lose them again.

blocks.markdown:
### Why federalism, and why Nigeria chose it

Federations are usually adopted where a country is large, diverse and suspicious of central domination. Nigeria's federalism grew out of exactly those pressures:

- **Size and population** — a country of over 923,000 square kilometres cannot be administered efficiently from one capital.
- **Ethnic and cultural diversity** — hundreds of language groups, with three large ones, made a single unitary centre unacceptable to all sides.
- **Fear of domination** — each major group feared being ruled by the others, so guaranteed regional powers were the price of unity.
- **Colonial inheritance** — the Richards Constitution of 1946 introduced regionalism, the Macpherson Constitution of 1951 deepened regional autonomy, and the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 formally made Nigeria a federation.
- **Uneven development** — regions at different economic levels wanted control over their own priorities.

items: **Merits of federalism** — it preserves unity while permitting diversity, brings government closer to the people, allows local priorities and experimentation, reduces the risk of central tyranny and accommodates minorities.

**Demerits of federalism** — it is expensive to run three tiers of government, it duplicates offices, it can generate conflict over revenue allocation and jurisdiction, and it may entrench regional or ethnic rivalry.
**Merits of a unitary system** — cheaper, faster decision making, uniform laws and standards, no jurisdictional disputes, and a strong sense of one nation.
**Demerits of a unitary system** — remoteness from local needs, overload at the centre, and the risk of tyranny where minority regions have no protected sphere.

blocks.markdown:
### How Nigeria's federal powers are divided

The Second Schedule to the 1999 Constitution contains two lists. The **Exclusive Legislative List** covers matters only the National Assembly may legislate on — defence, external affairs, currency, mines and minerals, customs, citizenship, aviation and the police, among others. The **Concurrent Legislative List** covers matters on which both the National Assembly and a State House of Assembly may legislate, such as education, health, agriculture, electricity and statistics; where a valid federal law and a state law conflict, the federal law prevails. Everything on neither list is a **residual** matter for the states alone, such as chieftaincy affairs and local markets.

blocks.title: Deciding which tier may legislate
blocks.prompt: Classify each subject as exclusive, concurrent or residual under the 1999 Constitution, and say which tier may act: (i) the currency; (ii) secondary education; (iii) the regulation of a local motor park.

steps.text: (i) Currency, coinage and legal tender appear on the Exclusive Legislative List, so only the National Assembly may legislate. A state cannot issue its own money.

(ii) Education appears on the Concurrent Legislative List, so both the National Assembly and a State House of Assembly may legislate — which is why Nigeria has both federal and state universities and colleges.
(iii) The regulation of a local motor park appears on neither list, so it is a residual matter for the state, which in practice assigns it to the local government council.
Apply the tie-breaker where relevant: on a concurrent matter, if the federal and state laws conflict, the federal law prevails and the state law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
Note the method: check the Exclusive List first, then the Concurrent List, and treat anything remaining as residual.

blocks.answer: (i) Exclusive — National Assembly only; (ii) Concurrent — both tiers, with federal law prevailing in a conflict; (iii) Residual — the state, usually through its local government councils

blocks.title: Federation versus confederation
blocks.text: The decisive difference is where sovereignty rests. In a federation the component units are not sovereign and cannot lawfully secede; in a confederation they remain sovereign and normally may withdraw. Say this explicitly and give the Senegambia Confederation of 1982 to 1989 as your confederal example.

points: A unitary system places all constitutional power at the centre, which delegates revocable functions to local units.
A federal system divides powers between centre and units by a written, rigid constitution, with a supreme court as arbiter.
A confederation is a loose union of sovereign states, whose members usually retain the right to secede.
Nigeria adopted federalism because of its size, ethnic diversity, fear of domination and the regionalism introduced from 1946 onwards.
The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 formally established Nigeria as a federation.
The 1999 Constitution divides powers into exclusive, concurrent and residual matters, with federal law prevailing on concurrent conflicts.
